799.title: In waves
799.hook: grief comes in waves, and research doesn't support neat "stages"
799.howItsDone: Grief counselors who work with the dual process model encourage people to let themselves turn toward the loss and then back to daily life, without treating the swing between them as going backward.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hold loosely: when death comes near the grip tightens, and noticing opens the hand. Your line was the hand closes. Now the path turns to grief.

A man is in the cereal aisle, some weeks after his mother's funeral, and he's fine. He's checking prices. Then he sees her brand of tea on the shelf, the one with the yellow box, and he's not fine at all. He stands there holding a basket, crying, while a stranger reaches politely around him for the oatmeal. By the checkout, he's making small talk with the cashier about the weather. If grief were a staircase, that aisle would look like falling back to the bottom. It isn't a staircase.
screen: `FINE IN THE CEREAL AISLE.` → `HER TEA ON THE SHELF.` → `SMALL TALK AT THE CHECKOUT.`

segments.voice: First, where the stages came from. The psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross spent time with dying patients and, in her book On Death and Dying, described stages she saw in them: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. She was writing about people facing their own death. The list traveled, and came to be used as a map for anyone grieving anyone. Second, what research on grieving people has found. Researchers have not found that grief moves through fixed stages in a set order. People differ, and one person can feel several things in an afternoon. Kübler-Ross herself later said the stages were never meant as a tidy sequence. Third, a better picture. The grief researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut describe grieving people moving back and forth: toward the loss, with its memories and tears, then toward ordinary life, cooking, paying the bills, laughing at something on television, then back again. They call it oscillation. In their model, the swing isn't a failure to grieve properly. It's how people cope. Fourth, an older poet found the same image. In Psalm 42, a singer far from home says: "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me." Waves rise, break over you, and pull back. Over time they can come further apart, though a big one can still arrive on an ordinary Tuesday, in a grocery aisle. Not stages. In waves.
screen: `THE STAGES BEGAN WITH THE DYING` · `GRIEF DOESN'T KEEP TO ORDER` · `TOWARD THE LOSS, THEN BACK TO LIFE` · `"ALL THY WAVES AND THY BILLOWS"` · then, large: `IN WAVES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a loss you can hold safely right now, a move, an ending, a friendship that faded, and if a large one feels too much today, choose a small one. Let the feeling rise a little, notice where it sits, the throat, the chest, behind the eyes, and breathe without pushing it down or stirring it up. Then gently turn toward something ordinary, the weight of the chair, your feet on the floor; that turning is part of grieving too.
In waves: grief rising and falling, toward the loss and back to life, rather than climbing a staircase of stages. Today's word.
Your line: deep calleth unto deep. A wave can come, and pass. Day seven hundred ninety-nine, done.

800.title: The bond continues
800.hook: many keep a bond with the dead, and grief researchers now see it as healthy
800.howItsDone: People keep bonds with the dead in many ways: Jewish families add "may their memory be a blessing" after a name, some Japanese Buddhist households greet the dead at a home altar, and others visit graves, keep a photo, or talk to the person on a walk.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was in waves: grief swinging toward the loss and back to life, not climbing stages. Your line was deep calleth unto deep.

A phone, a name in the contacts, and a message sent anyway: got the job. wish you could see. Nobody will answer. She knows that. She sends it anyway, puts the phone down, and feels a little less alone with the news. Somewhere else a man sets out his father's chair at the holiday table. A woman tells a gravestone about the new baby. For a long time, some schools of psychology would have called all of this a problem, a sign of grief not finished. What changed, and what were some traditions doing all along?
screen: `A TEXT TO A NUMBER THAT WON'T ANSWER.` → `A CHAIR AT THE TABLE.` → `A PROBLEM, OR A BOND?`

segments.voice: First, the older view. Healthy grief meant letting go: slowly loosening your ties to the person who died, so your heart was free to attach elsewhere. Some trace the idea to Freud's essay Mourning and Melancholia. Keeping up a relationship with the dead could look like refusing to accept the death. Second, the turn. The researchers Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman gathered studies of grieving people in a book called Continuing Bonds. People kept a relationship with their dead: talking to them, asking what they would think, carrying their values, feeling them near at a wedding. And this was often part of healthy grieving, not a failure of it. Researchers since have added a fair caution: some bonds comfort and some trouble, depending on the person and the loss. Third, traditions had words for this already. In Jewish custom, after naming someone who has died, people add a short phrase: may their memory be a blessing. In some Japanese Buddhist homes, a household altar called a butsudan holds photos and memorial tablets, and families greet the dead there, offer rice or tea, and tell them the news. Fourth, what continues is not the same as what was. The bond changes shape: from a voice on the phone to a voice in memory, from advice given to advice imagined, from a hand held to a value carried. The relationship moves. It doesn't have to end. The bond continues.
screen: `LET GO, SAID AN OLDER VIEW` · `CONTINUING BONDS` · `MAY THEIR MEMORY BE A BLESSING` · `THE BOND CHANGES SHAPE` · then, large: `THE BOND CONTINUES.`

segments.voice: Choose someone who has died, a person or even an animal, or if no one comes, an ancestor you never met, and let them come to mind as they were on an ordinary day. Silently tell them one thing, a piece of news, a thank-you, a question, then simply sit, the way you would after saying something to a friend across the table, no answer needed. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words.
Butsudan, the household altar in some Japanese Buddhist homes where family members greet their dead and tell them the news. Today's word.
Your line: a voice in memory. Staying in touch can take a new shape. Eight hundred days now.

801.title: Grieving an animal
801.hook: the loss of a pet is real grief
801.howItsDone: People mark the death of an animal in many ways: burying them in a garden, keeping a collar or a photo, planting something, or telling stories about them with family, and some vets and charities offer support for pet loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was butsudan, a home altar where families tell their dead the news. Your line was a voice in memory: the bond continues, in a new shape.

The water bowl is still by the back door. Nobody has moved it, because moving it would make it true. The leash hangs on its hook. Fur keeps turning up on a dark sweater, weeks later, and each time it's a small shock. The house is too quiet at the hour when someone used to wait by the door. Then a coworker says, kindly enough, it was just a dog, you can get another one. And the grief, which was real a minute ago, suddenly has nowhere to go.
screen: `THE BOWL BY THE BACK DOOR.` → `THE QUIET HOUR.` → `"IT WAS JUST A DOG."`

segments.voice: First, what was lost. A life with an animal is built out of daily things: the feeding, the walk in the rain, the weight at the end of the bed, being greeted at the door as if you'd been gone a year. When the animal dies, a whole shape of the day goes with it. Second, a name for grief that others don't count. The grief researcher Kenneth Doka called it disenfranchised grief: a loss the people around you don't recognize as worth mourning, so there's no card, no time off, no one asking how you are. An animal's death can fall there. Naming it doesn't fix it, but it can explain why the sadness feels lonely. Third, old texts paid attention to animals. Proverbs says: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." And a psalm praises God's care stretching wide: "O LORD, thou preservest man and beast." Traditions give different answers about what becomes of an animal after death, and those answers belong to each tradition. The question of grief is simpler: was the love real? Fourth, a poet who didn't hide it. When Lord Byron's dog Boatswain died, he had a monument raised at his family home and wrote verses for the stone, calling the dog his friend. People have mocked grief for animals, and people have built monuments for it. Either way, it comes from the same place as grief for a person.
screen: `A WHOLE SHAPE OF THE DAY` · `GRIEF OTHERS DON'T COUNT` · `"MAN AND BEAST"` · `A POET'S MONUMENT TO A DOG` · then, large: `LOVE WAS REAL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an animal you loved, your own, a childhood pet, a neighbor's dog that always came to the fence, and see one ordinary moment with them, the sound at the door, the warmth against your leg. Let yourself miss them, if you do, and silently say their name and one thing they gave you. If no animal comes to mind, think of one who belongs to someone you know, and how much that animal matters to them.
Disenfranchised grief, Kenneth Doka's name for a loss, like an animal's death, that others around you don't recognize as worth mourning. Today's word.
Your line: love was real. The bowl by the door can stay. That's day eight hundred one.

802.title: Before the loss
802.hook: grief can begin before a death, while caring for someone
802.howItsDone: Hospice teams and carers' support groups talk openly about anticipatory grief, and friends can help most with practical things: meals, errands, or a few hours of respite care.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was disenfranchised grief, a loss others don't count, like an animal's death. Your line was love was real.

Sunday night. A daughter sits at the kitchen table filling her mother's pill organizer, the way she has for months. Her mother is still here, in the next room, laughing at a game show. And the daughter is already grieving. Not for the woman in the next room, exactly, but for the one who used to drive, who remembered every birthday, who used to fill her own pills and would have hated needing help. Nobody sends flowers for that. There's no service for a loss that's still happening, one small piece at a time.
screen: `SUNDAY NIGHT, THE PILL ORGANIZER.` → `SHE'S STILL HERE.` → `THE GRIEF HAS ALREADY BEGUN.`

segments.voice: First, a name for it. The psychiatrist Erich Lindemann wrote about anticipatory grief: mourning that begins before a death, when a death is expected. People caring for someone with a long illness describe it as losing things one at a time: a shared joke the other person can't follow anymore, a role, a plan for later, the future they pictured. Second, it rarely comes alone. Carers describe love and tiredness side by side, sometimes a wish for the struggle to be over, and then guilt for having wished it. All of that can be in one heart in one evening. None of it cancels the love. Third, an old story of grief before and after. In the second book of Samuel, King David's young child falls ill. David fasts and lies all night on the ground. When the child dies, his servants are afraid to tell him. But David sees them whispering, understands, then gets up, washes, changes his clothes, and eats. Asked why, he says: "While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept," and then, "can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." His grief before looked one way, and his grief after another. Fourth, a caution. Grieving before a death doesn't mean the grief is used up when the death comes. Some find the after easier, some harder, some just different. Before doesn't cancel after.
screen: `GRIEF BEFORE A DEATH` · `LOVE AND TIREDNESS TOGETHER` · `DAVID FASTS, THEN RISES` · `BEFORE DOESN'T CANCEL AFTER` · then, large: `BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone caring for another person, a parent looking after a parent, someone nursing a partner, a friend with a sick child, or yourself, if the carer is you. Hold them in mind with no advice attached, just seeing them at the end of a long day. Then let one small kindness for them take shape, a message that needs no reply, a meal left at the door, an hour of sitting in so they can rest, and if you're the carer, let the kindness be for you.
Anticipatory grief, Erich Lindemann's name for mourning that begins before a death, as a carer loses things one at a time. Today's word.
Your line: before and after. Love and tiredness can share one heart in one evening. Until tomorrow.

803.title: Children and death
803.hook: children do best with plain, honest words
803.howItsDone: Children's grief centers and hospice programs coach parents to use the words died and dead, explain that the body has stopped working, answer questions briefly and honestly, and share the family's beliefs alongside the facts.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was anticipatory grief, mourning that starts before an expected death. Your line was before and after: one doesn't cancel the other.

A small boy is told that Grandpa went to sleep and won't wake up. That night, he won't get into bed. He fights it, crying, and nobody can work out why, until someone finally asks him, and he says he doesn't want to go to sleep like Grandpa. Across town, a little girl hears that the family lost Grandma, and she wants to know why nobody is out looking for her. The grown-ups chose soft words to protect them. The children took the words at their word.
screen: `GRANDPA WENT TO SLEEP.` → `THE BOY WON'T GO TO BED.` → `WHY ISN'T ANYONE LOOKING FOR GRANDMA?`

segments.voice: First, say died. Organizations that support grieving children, such as the Dougy Center in Portland, Oregon, advise using the real words, died and dead, and explaining them in a way a child can hold: the body stopped working. It doesn't breathe, eat, or feel pain anymore, and it can't start again. It sounds harsh to adult ears. To a child, it's something solid to stand on. Second, why soft words can backfire. Young children can take words literally. Asleep can make bedtime frightening. Lost suggests someone could be found. Went away can sound like a choice, or leave a child waiting at the window. The kindness meant can turn into fear or confusion. Third, short, honest, and again. Children may ask the same question many times, sometimes days apart, and may play happily one minute and cry the next. That doesn't mean they didn't understand. They're taking it in a bit at a time. The guidance: answer briefly and truthfully, as many times as it's asked, and say I don't know when you don't. Fourth, beliefs beside the fact, not instead of it. Families hold different beliefs about what follows death: heaven, rebirth, a return to God, or that nobody knows. Child grief guidance suggests sharing your family's beliefs alongside the plain fact. Grandma died. Her body stopped working. And then: here's what our family believes. The fact first, the belief beside it. Plain words.
screen: `SAY "DIED"` · `SOFT WORDS CAN FRIGHTEN` · `SHORT, HONEST, AND AGAIN` · `BELIEFS BESIDE THE FACT` · then, large: `PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of a death a child in your life might ask about, a grandparent, a neighbor, a goldfish, and quietly shape one sentence they could understand: the name, the word died, and one plain thing, like her body stopped working, so she can't come back. Notice any urge to soften it, and let the urge pass. Then add one warm, true line, such as we loved her, and we'll keep remembering her, and rest with the two sentences together.
Dougy Center, the organization that advises telling children the truth in plain words, died and dead, with warmth and room for questions. Today's word.
Your line: plain words. To a child, the plain word is solid ground. Day eight hundred three, done.

804.title: Rites hold us
804.hook: burial, cremation, Tibetan sky burial: each tradition's rite carries its own meaning
804.howItsDone: Funeral rites differ by tradition: Jewish and Muslim burial soon after death, Christian burial or cremation, Hindu and Sikh cremation, and in parts of Tibet sky burial, each carried out by the family and community in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Dougy Center, and its advice: tell children the truth in plain words. Your line was plain words.

Early morning on a high hillside in Tibet. A body, wrapped in cloth, is carried up to a flat place among the rocks. Monks have chanted. A man whose work this is prepares the body. Family members may watch from a distance, or go home. Then, out of a wide sky, the vultures come down. To someone from far away, it can look shocking. To the people who keep this rite, it carries a meaning of its own: the body is no longer needed, and so it is given, one last time, to living creatures.
screen: `A HILLSIDE IN TIBET.` → `THE VULTURES COME DOWN.` → `A LAST GIFT.`

segments.voice: First, the earth. In the Bible, God tells Adam: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Jewish and Muslim traditions call for burying the body in the ground, traditionally soon after death, simply and with care. Christian burial carries the hope of resurrection, and some Christians choose cremation. The grave says: the body goes back to where it came from. Second, the fire. Hindu and Sikh families traditionally cremate. In Hindu understanding the fire returns the body to the elements and frees the one who lived in it; a close family member, by tradition a son, lights the pyre. The fire says: what was here is released. Third, the birds. In Tibetan Buddhist understanding, consciousness has already left the body, so what remains is an empty vessel. Offering it to the vultures is a final act of generosity, feeding other beings, and a plain lesson in impermanence for those who watch. In Tibetan it's called jhator, giving alms to the birds. The sky says: even this can be given. Fourth, what they share. Each rite gives the mourners something to do with their hands at the moment they least know what to do: shovel the earth, carry the body, light the fire, walk up the hill. It tells them where to stand, what to say, who goes first. When nobody can think, the rite does some of the thinking. Different rites, each belonging to its people, and in each of them, rites hold us.
screen: `DUST TO DUST` · `THE FIRE THAT RELEASES` · `ALMS FOR THE BIRDS` · `SOMETHING FOR THE HANDS TO DO` · then, large: `RITES HOLD US.`

segments.voice: Choose a tradition's funeral rite, one different from the one you grew up with, or your own if you've never looked at it closely, and gather what you already know: who washes the body, who carries it, what is said, and by whom. Notice, too, what you don't know. Then hold the people who keep that rite with respect, the way you'd want your own held.
Jhator, the Tibetan rite of giving the body as alms to the birds, one of several rites that hold mourners when they least know what to do. Today's word.
Your line: even this can be given. Earth, fire or sky, each rite carries its own meaning. Rest well.

805.title: Six words
805.hook: an epitaph is a life in a line
805.carry: a life pressed into a line
805.howItsDone: Families choose epitaphs with care: sometimes a line of scripture, a favorite phrase, or a few words that sum up a life, and some people write their own long before they're needed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was jhator, the Tibetan rite of giving a body to the birds. Your line was even this can be given.

A small cemetery in Amherst, Massachusetts. A plain stone behind an iron fence, with a name on it, Emily Dickinson, her dates, and just two words: Called Back. Across an ocean, in a cemetery in Rome, a stone does the opposite. It doesn't give the name at all. It calls the man beneath it a young English poet, and gives a line he asked for: "Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water." That's John Keats. One stone says almost nothing. The other leaves out the one thing a gravestone usually gives. Both say a great deal: a life in a line.
screen: `AMHERST: "CALLED BACK."` → `ROME: NO NAME AT ALL.` → `A LIFE IN A LINE.`

segments.voice: First, what an epitaph is for. It's a life pressed into a line and cut into stone, and it isn't for the dead. It's for whoever walks by later: a grandchild, a stranger, someone looking for shade. It answers one question for them: who was this? Second, Called Back. Dickinson's stone holds just those words under her name and dates, and it's said she used them in one of her last notes to her cousins. Some readers hear a summons, someone being called home; others hear something quieter, like a child called in from playing at dusk. The stone doesn't explain. Third, a name writ in water. Keats, dying young and, by his friends' account, sure his poems would be forgotten, asked for that line and no name. His friends kept the name off, though they added bitter words of their own about his enemies above it. Water doesn't hold writing. People still walk to his grave to read the line about vanishing, its own small irony. Fourth, six words, because six is short enough to force a choice. Not a résumé, not a list of jobs: what would you want someone in the shade to know? That closes a week of grief: waves that come and go, a bond that continues, love for an animal that was real, grief before and after, plain words for children, rites that hold us. And now the shortest thing a life can leave: six words.
screen: `A LIFE IN A LINE` · `"CALLED BACK"` · `A NAME WRIT IN WATER` · `A WEEK OF GRIEF` · then, large: `SIX WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let a few words come about the life you're actually living, not the one on paper, and try one line of six, counting them on your fingers. Too many, cut one; not quite true, change it; it can be funny, plain, or a little odd. When one fits, say it once in your head, and let it rest.
Six words: a life pressed into one short line, the way an epitaph speaks to whoever walks by later. Today's word.
Your line: a life pressed into a line. Six words can hold more than they seem. Day eight hundred five closes the week.
